register.name: Minnesota Office of the Revisor of Statutes - Minnesota Statutes (official publisher)
register.access_notes: Fetched cleanly over HTTPS with an honest identifying user agent ('canon-legislation-indexer/1.0 (legalese/canon metadata research; michael.fairweather@gmail.com)'), requests spaced ~2 seconds apart; about 20 requests in total. No robots block, no challenge, no 403/429. Working URL patterns: chapter page /statutes/cite/<chapter> (e.g. /statutes/cite/177), full chapter text /statutes/<year>/cite/<chapter>/full, section page /statutes/cite/<section>. Note: /statutes/chapter/<n>, /statutes/part/<n> and /copyright/ do not exist (404). Two transient connection failures (curl exit 28 / empty response) on /statutes/info and /statutes/cite/181.13/pdf were worked around simply by retrying the same page through a different fetcher, not by changing identity. The site carries no copyright notice and no terms-of-use page that I could find.

licence.summary: No copyright is asserted over Minnesota Statutes on the register. The chapter and section pages carry no copyright notice, there is no terms-of-use or copyright page (/copyright/ returns 404), and the 'About Minnesota Statutes' page addresses only official/authentic status, not reuse. The Revisor's office is the official publisher (not a commercial publisher), and current Minn. Stat. ch. 3C contains no copyright provision - only s. 3C.13, which makes certified volumes prima facie evidence, and s. 3C.10, subd. 3, which permits contracting a commercial publisher for editing/printing of the print edition. Under the government edicts doctrine (Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020)) the statutory text itself is not copyrightable, so reuse and adaptation of the text are permitted. Treated as open. Human check: the print edition is produced under contract and older editions bore a 'Revisor of Statutes, State of Minnesota' copyright line; anyone reusing the print/annotated edition rather than the free web text should confirm that separately.

register.name: Mississippi Code of 1972 Annotated - 'Mississippi Code Public Access', hosted on LexisNexis Advance for the Joint Legislative Committee on Compilation, Revision and Publication of Legislation (linked as the code source by both the Mississippi Legislature and the Secretary of State)
register.access_notes: Mississippi has no state-run consolidated code website. The Legislature's own site (https://www.legislature.ms.gov/) carries only bill/measure search; its single code link points off-site to http://www.lexisnexis.com/hottopics/mscode/, which redirects to the LexisNexis Advance 'Mississippi Code Public Access' container. Scripted access is impossible: curl of the redirect target returns a JavaScript 'cookiesrequired' bounce, and https://www.sos.ms.gov/publications-external-affairs/mississippi-law returns HTTP 403 to curl (it was readable through the Claude WebFetch tool). Verification was therefore done in a real interactive Chrome browser on the public-access platform, with no sign-in: about 4 page loads plus 2 searches. IMPORTANT: when I clicked through from the search-results list to a full document view, the platform served a 'Captcha Validation' page ('We use CAPTCHA on this site to prevent automated software from overburdening the system...'). I stopped there and did not attempt, solve or work around the CAPTCHA, so no full document page was opened and no per-document 'current through <session>' currency statement could be captured. Everything recorded below comes from the code's own live table of contents and search-result headers on that platform, seen before the challenge.

licence.summary: Not open. Mississippi is the strongest copyright assertion of the group: the Secretary of State states that the laws of Mississippi are copyrighted by the State of Mississippi, citing Miss. Code Ann. s. 1-1-9, and that section (seen in the code's own search results) provides that copyright in the Mississippi Code of 1972 and its notes, annotations and indexes is taken in the publisher's name and then assigned to, and owned by, the State. The official code is published under contract by LexisNexis (Michie) for the Joint Legislative Committee on Compilation, Revision and Publication of Legislation, and the public-access platform footers read 'Copyright (c) 2026 LexisNexis.' with its own 'Terms & Conditions'. Against that: under the government edicts doctrine (Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020)) the enacted statutory text itself is not copyrightable no matter what the State asserts, so the words of the sections may be reused and adapted; what is realistically protected is the publisher's apparatus (annotations, editorial notes, indexes, the platform's own formatting) and what is contractually restricted is bulk use of the LexisNexis platform under its Terms & Conditions. open_licence is set false because neither the State nor the publisher grants reuse-and-adaptation rights, and there is no state-run source to take the text from. A human must decide whether to rely on the government edicts doctrine here and should read the LexisNexis Terms & Conditions before any bulk extraction.

Wrongful Discharge From Employment - Table of Contents, Title 39, Chapter 2, MCA', headings 'TITLE 39' / 'CHAPTER 2' / 'Part 9', with a live sections index and no repeal marker.
acts.notes: Montana is the only US state that has displaced pure at-will employment by statute, so this is a genuinely state-law topic here rather than a gap. It caps damages and provides a discharge remedy; it does not mandate severance pay.
